title-group.article-title: A Model‐Based Approach to Evaluate Anti‐Drug Antibody Impact on Drug Exposure With Biologics: A Case Example With the CD3 T‐Cell Bispecific Cibisatamab

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: The administration of biologics can lead to immunogenic responses that trigger anti‐drug antibody (ADA) formation. ADAs can decrease drug exposure. A population pharmacokinetic (popPK) model was developed to describe clinical PK data with and without ADA‐driven exposure loss with CEA‐directed T‐cell bispecific antibody cibisatamab. The PK of cibisatamab was evaluated in two clinical studies (as a single agent and in combination with the checkpoint inhibitor atezolizumab) in patients. The popPK model was developed on cibisatamab clinical PK data using the Stochastic Approximation –Expectation Maximization (SAEM) algorithm implemented in Monolix. Cibisatamab's PK followed a two‐compartment model with linear clearance decreasing over time and ADA‐associated exposure loss. ADA‐driven exposure loss was implemented in the model by accounting for ADA formation, reversible binding to cibisatamab, and elimination of both free ADA and the ADA‐cibisatamab complex from the central compartment. The impact of ADAs on PK exposure was time‐dependent in the model, with the ADA formation described as a function of time (increasing from zero, reaching its estimated maximum value, and possibly decreasing down to 94% of this maximum value in some patients). The final model included a mixture component differentiating patients with and without exposure loss due to ADA formation (75% and 25% of patients, respectively). The investigated patient demographics, dose or dosing schedule, or atezolizumab coadministration were not identified as factors influencing exposure loss due to ADAs. The developed model can be used to differentiate patients with and without ADA‐driven exposure loss, as well as for a precise PK characterization in patients even with ADA formation.

sec.p: Keywords: anti‐drug antibodies, bispecific antibody, modeling, population pharmacokinetics

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Administration of biologic drugs in humans can lead to the development of anti‐drug antibodies (ADAs). ADA development can be associated with decreased exposure.

What question did this study address? ○
A population PK analysis was conducted to establish the dose‐exposure relationship and quantify the impact of ADAs in drug exposure using the case example of cibisatamab, a CEA‐directed CD3 T‐cell bispecific.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
A model was developed that can differentiate between patients with or without ADA‐driven exposure loss. In the example with cibisatamab, the model predicted that 75% of patients show some extent of exposure loss due to ADAs. The model is also able to describe exposure recovery over time (transient ADA‐associated loss of exposure), which occurred in 53% of the patients with ADA‐driven exposure loss treated with cibisatamab. This approach can be used to evaluate the effect of patient covariates, dose, or dosing schedule on ADA‐driven exposure loss. In this analysis, these factors were not found to be associated with ADA‐induced loss of exposure.

How might this change drug discovery, development, and/or therapeutics? ○
The developed model is able to accurately describe the PK profile in all treated patients, both with and without ADA‐associated exposure loss. This is a prerequisite to developing robust PK/PD models, necessary for successful drug development. Similar models can be developed for biologics with ADA‐associated impact on PK.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The use of biologic drugs has transformed the treatment landscape across multiple therapeutic areas [1, 2]. In the context of cancer immunotherapy, T‐cell bispecifics (TCBs) are antibodies capable of binding to the CD3 receptor on T‐cell surface and to a tumor‐associated antigen on the tumor cell [3]. Cibisatamab (RO6958688) is a TCB directed toward the CEA antigen [4], which is overexpressed in multiple solid malignancies [5]. Cibisatamab has been studied in heavily pretreated patients with solid tumors, both as a single agent, as well as in combination with the anti‐PD‐L1 checkpoint inhibitor atezolizumab (Tecentriq), or with the bispecific 4‐1BB costimulator FAP‐4‐1BBL (RO7122290). Preliminary pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data, as well as early results on the safety and efficacy of both cibisatamab single agent and cibisatamab combined with atezolizumab, have been described [6]. In these studies, anti‐drug antibodies (ADAs) have been noted to affect cibisatamab's exposure in patients.

Although treatment with TCBs has revolutionized multiple hematological malignancies [7, 8, 9, 10], success in solid tumors has so far proven more elusive. To improve success, understanding the dose‐exposure and exposure‐response relationship as early as possible with TCBs is beneficial. With respect to dose‐exposure, population pharmacokinetic (popPK) analysis has become a standard in the field [11]. Monoclonal antibodies, such as TCBs, present additional challenges when evaluating the dose‐exposure relationship, such as the development of anti‐drug antibodies (ADA) potentially impacting the PK of the drug. ADA formation has been shown to impact drug exposure and lead to decreased efficacy [12, 13, 14]. In other cases, despite high rates of ADA formation, a moderate or no effect on drug exposure, as well as no impact on drug efficacy, has been found [15, 16, 17]. Furthermore, ADA formation during treatment with biologics has also been associated with a higher risk of infusion‐related reactions and other adverse events [12, 18].

Given the impact of ADAs on both safety and efficacy, several initiatives are aiming to predict the immunogenicity of novel biologics by leveraging both preclinical data and mathematical modeling approaches [19]. Furthermore, mathematical models aiming to describe both mechanistically and empirically ADA occurrence and impact on drug exposure in the clinic have been suggested [20, 21, 22]. In those cases where a relationship between exposure and immunogenicity is found, the models can be used to propose dosing regimens limiting ADA formation. In this work, we focus on developing a PK model on cibisatamab clinical PK data, where exposure was impacted by ADA formation.

Some population pharmacokinetic models have already been proposed for different TCBs [23, 24, 25]. In those cases, the ADA incidence was low, as these TCBs can also deplete B cells. Here, we develop a popPK model characterizing the pharmacokinetics of cibisatamab in patients with advanced cancer whose tumors express the CEA antigen. In addition, the differences in ADA formation and ADA impact on cibisatamab's exposure as a function of patient covariates, dose, and dosing schedule, and coadministration of cibisatamab with atezolizumab were also explored. This model was thereafter used to evaluate the dose‐exposure relationships using the totality of the data.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic (PK) Data and Population Characteristics
sec.p: PK samples were available from two cibisatamab studies. Study BP29541 (NCT02324257) was the first‐in‐human trial for cibisatamab, which was conducted in patients with advanced, CEA‐positive solid tumors, and had cibisatamab's pharmacokinetic data from 143 patients [26]. Of these 143 patients, 27 patients received obinutuzumab pretreatment with the goal of depleting B cells and diminishing ADA formation. Study WP29945 (NCT02650713) evaluated cibisatamab in combination with atezolizumab in patients with advanced, CEA‐positive solid tumors, and had cibisatamab PK data from 228 patients. No patient received obinutuzumab pretreatment in this study. Details on the study protocols have been previously described [6].

The dataset for modeling consisted of 11,341 samples from 371 patients with advanced solid tumors. Patients received at least one dose of cibisatamab intravenously, either as a single agent with varying dosing frequencies (every week [qw] to every 3 weeks [q3w]) (NCT02324257) or in combination with atezolizumab at a dose of 1200 mg q3w (NCT03866239). Table 1 summarizes patients' demographics, as well as other characteristics of the clinical trials. Detailed information on ADA positivity per dose cohort is available in the (Table S1).

sec.title: Analytical Methods
sec.p: Cibisatamab serum concentrations were determined using a dual target binding enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) which measured concentrations of unbound cibisatamab. The assay specifications slightly differed between patients enrolled in the monotherapy dose‐escalation study (NCT02650713) and the atezolizumab combination dose‐escalation study (NCT03866239). The lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) in the monotherapy study was 0.925 ng/mL, whereas it was 2 ng/mL in the atezolizumab combination study. Intra‐assay accuracy was between 90.1% and 107.2%, and the imprecision did not exceed a 15.6% coefficient of variation (CV).

The presence of ADA was evaluated using a bridging ELISA with high sensitivity. The ADA assay used to evaluate the samples from the study of cibisatamab in combination with atezolizumab had improved drug tolerance. In turn, ADA detection and quantification were less affected by cibisatamab [6] in the combination study compared to the assay used to evaluate the samples from the study of cibisatamab in monotherapy. As a result, ADA positivity rates were not directly comparable between the two studies. The observed ADA titers were not included in the model building, but the relationship to the model‐predicted loss of drug exposure was explored graphically. For this, cibisatamab monotherapy was assessed separately from cibisatamab plus atezolizumab combination as the ADA determination assay differed between the two studies.

sec.title: PK Modeling
sec.p: Model development was conducted in Monolix 2023R1 [27] using the stochastic approximation‐expectation maximization (SAEM) algorithm. Goodness of fit (GoF) plots, model simulations, and model exploration were performed in R version 4.2.1 [28] using the rxode2 package [29]. Final model selection was performed based on GoF plots, prediction‐corrected visual predictive checks (pcVPCs), precision of parameter estimates, and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). The Fisher Information Matrix was estimated with the Stochastic Approximation, and the Objective Function Value (OFV) was calculated using Importance Sampling. Observations below the limit of quantification were handled using the M4 method [30, 31].

sec.title: Model Development
sec.p: First, a base model was developed to describe cibisatamab's PK properties using the data from patients for whom the bioanalytical assay detected no ADAs at any time point and, in addition, whose concentration‐time profiles revealed no apparent reduction of exposure over time (see Data S1). On this reduced data set, consisting of 116 patients, compartmental models with different elimination functions linear, Michaelis–Menten, combined linear/Michaelis Menten, time‐varying clearance [32] were tested to inform the basic model structure.

Next, once cibisatamab's PK under no ADA impact on PK was elucidated, the impact of ADAs on cibisatamab's elimination was explored using all data available. In all cases, ADAs were assumed to bind cibisatamab only in the central compartment, with a 1:1 stoichiometry, and both free ADAs (unbound to cibisatamab) and the ADA‐cibisatamab complex were assumed to share the same elimination constant. Different model structures were tested to account for the ADA impact on PK, including the Michaelis–Menten approximation to target‐mediated drug disposition, increased clearance over time as a result of neutralizing ADA formation, as well as earlier suggested semi‐mechanistic models [22, 33].

Finally, a mixture model was also investigated on all available patient PK data. The mixture was implemented on the ADA formation constant parameter (estimated versus fixed to zero), and patient classification was based on a latent (unknown) covariate [34] (see Data S1).

The model for residual unexplained variability (RUV) was selected based on residual plots using the totality of the data, AIC, and RUV parameter estimates. Additive, proportional, and combined (additive plus proportional) error models were tested. As the SAEM algorithm requires inter‐individual variability (IIV) on all parameters to draw samples from their marginal distributions, IIV was included for all parameters, although it was fixed to a low value (⍵ = 0.1) for the Max_decrease parameter. No interoccasion variability was considered during model development.

Shrinkage of the Empirical Bayes Estimates (EBEs) was calculated as the ratio between the standard deviation of the EBEs and the estimated omega for that parameter, and epsilon‐shrinkage was calculated using the standard deviation of the individual weighted residuals (IWRES) [35].

sec.title: Loss of Exposure Analysis
sec.p: The patterns of drug exposure loss as a result of ADA formation, as well as their relationship to patient covariates, dose, and dosing schedules, were explored by simulations. sec.title: Final popPK Model
sec.p: When the base model was fitted to the reduced dataset with patients without ADA‐driven loss of exposure (see Materials and Methods section 2), a two‐compartment model with time‐decreasing clearance [32] from the central compartment (Equation 4) best‐described cibisatamab's PK.

Clearance (Equation 4) was described as a combination of a constant component (CLconst) and a component decreasing mono‐exponentially with time since the first dose, involving CLvar and λ parameters. The typical maximum decrease in clearance over time was 48% of the total initial clearance, and the typical half‐life of the decreasing clearance was 23 days. Equation (5) describes both the regular PK of cibisatamab (distribution and elimination), as well as the reversible binding to ADAs. Equation (6) describes the distribution of free cibisatamab to the peripheral compartment.
where A1 and A2, V1 and V2 denote the amounts and volumes of distribution of the central and peripheral compartments, respectively. CL and Q denote the central and intercompartmental clearances.

For the full dataset, the ADA‐driven loss of exposure was accounted for by including ADA formation, ADA binding to cibisatamab in the central compartment, and elimination of both free ADA and ADA‐cibisatamab complexes in the central compartment. Only free cibisatamab was assumed to be distributed to the peripheral compartment. Figure 2a schematically depicts the final structural model. The ADA data were excluded from the PK model because ADA titers did not reliably predict drug exposure, and additional clarifying data (total drug exposure, detailed ADA characterization) were unavailable. Also, during the model development, no link between ADA formation and dose, schedule, or other prior patient information could be identified (e.g., through post hoc parameters, Figure 5). Formation of ADAs was described by the ksyn parameter, which follows a bell‐shaped relationship versus time (Equation 7), (Figure 2a), and ranges from zero at the start of treatment to ksynMAX. During the ascending phase of ksyn versus time, T50,ksyn increase represents the time at which ksyn reaches half of ksynMAX. ksyn can subsequently decrease (thus reflecting transient ADA formation) up to a maximum percentage termed Maxdecrease. The time at which ksyn has decreased to half of its maximum decrease (Maxdecrease) occurs at the sum of T50,ksyn decrease and T50,ksyn increase. The steepness of the ksyn function versus time is described by the HillADA parameter. Once formed in the central compartment, ADAs bind to cibisatamab with rate constant kon, forming a complex (Complex) which dissociates back to free ADAs and free cibisatamab with rate constant koff. Both the free ADAs and the Complex are eliminated from the central compartment with rate constant kout,ADA (Equations 8 and 9).

sec.p: The final parameter estimates and their associated relative standard error (RSE) obtained by stochastic approximation are shown in Table 2. The model precision of parameter estimates showed no RSEs above 40%, and no major model misspecifications were apparent from observations versus predictions, residuals, and pcVPC plots. Large IIV was estimated for many of the parameters related to ADA formation and elimination, as well as the ADA binding affinity to cibisatamab (k on in Table 2).

sec.p: Instead of using a fixed allometric exponent, the relationship to body weight was estimated, as this provided a more accurate description of the data. Body weight was the only covariate with a statistically significant impact on a PK parameter (central volume of distribution). The estimation of the exponent (β) for the impact of body weight on the central volume of distribution (Equation 1) significantly improved model performance versus standard allometric scaling with a fixed exponent of 1. GoF and pcVPC (Figure 2b,c) demonstrated a reasonable fit of the developed model to the data. Additional diagnostic plots are available in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: ADA Formation and Impact on Cibisatamab's Exposure
sec.p: Several patterns of loss of exposure due to ADA formation were apparent both from data visualization, as well as from inspection of the individual fits. Figure 3 displays three representative individuals (belonging to the higher, medium, and lower tertile of RUV [computed as the standard deviation of the IWRES]) from four different categories: no loss of exposure, total loss of exposure (PK samples after end of infusion below LLOQ), loss of exposure during the dosing interval (PK samples in the elimination phase below LLOQ), and transient loss of exposure (exposure loss followed by exposure recovery at later dosing cycles).

caption.p: Examples of representative individual fits showcasing different patterns of loss of drug exposure due to ADA formation. Points represent observations, and lines represent the individual model predictions. Gray shaded area represents concentration values below the limit of quantification. Three individuals per group are shown, with one belonging to the higher, medium, and lower tertile of residual unexplained variability (RUV).

sec.p: Among patients enrolled in Study BP29541 (cibisatamab monotherapy), those who received obinutuzumab pretreatment were assigned by the model in a higher proportion to the “No ADA formation” (13/27 [48%] patients, compared to 26/116 [22%] of the patients who did not receive obinutuzumab pretreatment). For those patients who received obinutuzumab pretreatment and were assigned by the model to the “ADA formation” category, the median LOEav (average loss of exposure, calculated as detailed in Figure 1) was found to be lower than for the patients who did not receive obinutuzumab pretreatment (25% vs. 54%).
LOEav was found to be independent of dose, dosing schedule, or atezolizumab coadministration, as well as being independent of patient covariates, as illustrated in Figure 4.

sec.title: ADA Titers and Exposure Loss
sec.p: In general, measured ADA titers were qualitatively correlated with model‐predicted exposure loss (Figure 5a). Figure 5b illustrates the heterogeneity in terms of PK profile and change in ADA titer over time. For instance, Patient 4 shows an increase in ADA titer around day 15 after treatment start, which is approximately the time when the PK profile starts showing ADA‐associated exposure loss. Patient 3 shows no ADA‐associated exposure loss, which is in agreement with the observed PK profile. Conversely, Patient 6 and Patient 8 illustrate how ADA titers are not always predictive of exposure loss (ADA titers detectable in Patient 8 without exposure loss, and no ADA titers detectable for Patient 6 despite a PK profile suggesting ADA‐driven exposure loss). Specifically, 29 patients in Study 29,541 (cibisatamab monotherapy) and 20 patients in Study 29,945 (cibisatamab plus atezolizumab combination) had no quantifiable ADA titers while in the study, despite displaying loss of exposure according to their observed PK and model‐derived individual PK profiles. The model‐predicted mean LOEav during treatment was found to be 18.5% and 23.8%, respectively, for these patients.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: A PK model capable of describing different patterns of exposure loss due to ADA formation was developed on clinical data using the case example of the bispecific antibody cibisatamab. We used a mixture model to differentiate patients with and without ADA‐driven exposure loss. An alternative approach, such as hidden Markov models [36], could potentially reveal relationships between ADA formation and patients' characteristics, though this was not explored in this analysis.

In patients with ADA‐driven loss of exposure, the model can describe complete loss of exposure (PK samples after the end of infusion below LLOQ), loss of exposure during the dosing interval (PK samples in the elimination phase below LLOQ), and transient loss of exposure (exposure loss followed by exposure recovery at later dosing cycles). The ability to appropriately predict plasma exposure with biologics, in particular in the presence of ADA‐induced exposure loss, is a prerequisite to characterize the exposure‐response relationship through pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) modeling.

It is important when developing a PK model in the presence of ADAs to distinguish the ADA contribution to PK behavior versus any other nonlinear processes. Our approach was to first detect any nonlinear behavior based on the data where we had evidence of the absence of ADAs. In this initial phase, it is critical for the model to capture well any nonlinear processes and make sure that they are not confounded later with the nonlinear PK behavior associated with ADA formation.

We assumed ADAs bind to cibisatamab in a 1:1 ratio and that both free ADAs and the ADA‐cibisatamab complex share the same elimination constant. However, larger ADA‐drug complexes clear faster than smaller ones [37], which warrant further investigation.

The dissociation parameter (k off) between the TCB and ADAs was fixed at 0.1 day–1. A sensitivity analysis on this parameter (tested range from 0 to 10, data not shown) revealed that a value of 0.1 day‐1 lead to the best fit. When building such models, we recommend generating evidence on the binding properties of ADAs to a given IgG (e.g., in vitro binding assays) as this information can be difficult to infer from PK data.

In this study, patient covariates (sex, body weight, age, atezolizumab coadministration), dose, and dosing regimen were not identified to be predictive of ADA‐associated exposure loss (similar conclusion as previously described cases in oncology [38]). The model could therefore not be used to optimize treatment conditions by minimizing ADA formation. Obinutuzumab pretreatment prior to the administration of cibisatamab showed a trend toward more patients without ADA‐driven exposure loss (48% vs. 22%) and also decreased extent of exposure loss (25% vs. 54%) compared to cibisatamab monotherapy. This finding is in agreement with results from other studies [39], albeit the number of patients pretreated with obinutuzumab in our study (n = 27) was low.

Previous work [26] suggested that cibisatamab exposure is more suited to interpreting the impact of ADAs than using ADA titer data. Indeed, ADA status (i.e., bioanalytical assessment of the presence or not of ADAs in patient serum) was found to not always explain the observed PK profiles, and since the method to assess ADA differed between the included studies, ADA status was intentionally not used as a covariate during the model building process. Measuring neutralizing and binding ADAs, as well as the ADA‐cibisatamab immune complexes, would help interpret cibisatamab exposure observed in patients. In this context, a total PK assay would provide valuable insight for the development of a more mechanistic PK model. Also, a PK model including both PK and ADA data would allow for real‐time decisions on a patient's treatment continuation based on ADA data and reduce overall ADA formation. A PK model that incorporates ADA (and total PK) data can help differentiate the impact of ADA on drug exposure from other time‐dependent confounding factors.

The developed model infers that unexplained PK behavior (mainly increased clearance of cibisatamab) is associated with the presence of ADAs in patients. As a result, the model can infer quantitative insights on the extent of ADA formation and their binding properties. The model was found to detect more patients with ADA‐associated exposure less than the number of patients with at least one sample with ADA titers not equal to zero (75% vs. 59%). Also, more than half (53%) of the patients with ADA‐associated exposure loss showed some extent of drug exposure recovery during the time they remained under treatment. This indicates that the number of neutralizing ADAs can reduce over time in these patients, similar to what has already been noted for other biologics [40, 41]. In the case of atezolizumab, prior studies have found little impact of ADAs both on exposure and pharmacological effect [16, 42].

In this work, the model‐based approach detected more patients with ADA formation than the extensive ADA titer measurements during the clinical studies. Combining the current modeling approach with fewer ADA measurements during clinical studies could be enough to characterize ADA occurrence or its effect on exposure in patients. In addition, using a model‐based approach can assess the impact of immunogenicity on drug exposure independently of the bioanalytical assay used to evaluate ADA titers. For instance, different assays to assess ADAs can be used at different stages of the drug development process, with different performances when evaluating the presence of ADAs in patients' serum. The proposed model‐based approach should be complementary to the existing approach (bioanalytical methods) and should be re‐evaluated with more cases.

The ADA‐associated loss of exposure to biologics can trigger a loss of pharmacological activity and subsequently contribute to the large attrition rate during clinical studies [13, 14]. It is crucial to understand the probability and extent of ADA‐driven exposure loss with biologics early in drug development. Doing so would prevent having a large number of patients with no therapeutic benefit and continuing clinical development programs for longer than required. Additionally, the model provides suitable individual PK simulations, even over long treatment durations, which is critical to establishing the pharmacological effect versus exposure relationship. In addition, the developed model presents the advantage of no data exclusion, as patients with ADA‐induced exposure loss can still have an accurately described PK profile and can be included in PK/PD models subsequently. By including all patients in the analysis, the amount of information available is maximized and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the dose‐exposure relationship. In the particular case of oncology, it is critical to distinguish loss of efficacy due to loss of drug exposure from the development of treatment resistance. Such loss of efficacy coupled with loss of exposure has already been described for TCBs [13].

At the individual patient level, the model was capable of describing varied PK profiles (total loss of exposure [PK samples after end of infusion below LLOQ], loss of exposure at Ctrough [PK samples in the elimination phase below LLOQ], and transient loss of exposure [exposure is lost due to ADAs during some time period, but subsequently recovers]). Because no patient characteristic or effect of dosing schedule was identified on ADA formation and the impact on exposure, the model cannot be used to a priori predict the risk of a given patient of ADA‐driven exposure loss, or how this exposure loss can be mitigated via changes in dose or dosing schedule.

We have presented a model that quantifies the ADA‐driven exposure loss for the biologic cibisatamab. This model would benefit from additional validation using external datasets. We believe that similar models could be more extensively used to characterize the exposure–response relationship during the drug development of biologics. Similar models can be developed on preclinical data to characterize the exposure–response relationship before human trials, to assess whether further molecule development is warranted from the PK/PD perspective. Additionally, the use of similar models, which allow inclusion of all patients regardless of ADA status in exposure–response analysis, can be used to, for example, power a phase III clinical study (how many patients are needed to show a statistically significant benefit). These models allow using the totality of the data, and by consequence the totality of evidence generated all along drug development.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: A popPK model has been developed using the case example of cibisatamab. The model is capable of differentiating patients with or without ADA‐driven loss of exposure and can describe different PK profiles in the presence of ADAs. In the case of cibisatamab, no patient characteristic or effect of the dosing regimen was found on ADA‐driven loss of exposure. A moderate correlation between measured ADA titers and model‐predicted exposure loss was found. We recommend that similar models be developed and used to characterize immunogenicity with other biologics.
